*Numbers below come from the full report (`report_nedlame_treatment_comparison_clean.html`), which has the methods, figures and limits. This is a summary for discussion, not a standalone analysis.*

## The pilot

The farm is testing a Nedap camera that flags cows with reduced mobility. A flag creates a `NEDLAME` event in DairyComp. Flagged cows go to one of two arms: **TX**, trimmed automatically off the alert, or **Control**, where staff decide whether to act. Cows are randomised to arm by lactation group.

- 1,109 cows were flagged between 2026-06-02 and 2026-09-07, about 14 weeks
- 170 were dropped because the alert landed 1-7 days *after* a trim (see below)
- That leaves **939 cows: 441 TX and 498 Control**

Alerts come in three types: **`LOW`** (absolute mobility score in the lowest band), **`LOW DECLINE`** and **`STRONG DECLINE`** (a drop against the cow's own history). These are three different triggers with different enrollment rules, not three severity levels.

Everything here is descriptive. No significance testing, deliberately — the point is discussion.

## A timing problem worth knowing about

`NEDLAME`'s daily import runs at ~5am and stamps each alert with the day it was **loaded**, not the day the camera saw the cow. Trim records are often entered a day or two late. Put together, an alert dated 1-7 days after a trim is usually the camera picking up soreness from that trim, not a new problem.

The 170 cows whose *first* alert fits this pattern (15.3% of all alerts) are excluded from the comparisons above and reported separately.

## Findings

1. **Milk** — no separation between arms. TX 93.8% of baseline at day 30, Control 93.6%. See the caveat below: this rests on a minority of the cohort.

2. **Time to next trim** — TX reaches a follow-up trim in 90.9% of cases within 30 days vs 36.9% for Control. Expected, since TX auto-trims. But **about half of TX's first visits find nothing** (54.1% trim-only, vs 45.5% for Control).

3. **Farm staff** — staff flag cows on their own at much the same rate in both arms (Control 19.3%, TX 18.1%). The camera runs alongside staff, not instead of them.

4. **Lameness history** — 359 of 939 cows (38.2%) carry a `Chronic` label. That is mostly how the classifier defines chronic (any 2nd diagnosis more than a day apart), not evidence of active recurring problems. Only 3 cows are `Repeat`, all from a one-day gap — a timing artifact.

5. **Culling** — Control 28 of 498 (5.6%), TX 25 of 441 (5.7%). Indistinguishable.

6. **What the camera missed** — of 675 cows with a lesion diagnosed since June 1, **406 (60.1%) had no NEDAP alert in DairyComp in the 21 days before diagnosis.** Cases where the system structurally could not alert (heifers, dry cows, cows trimmed in the last 28 days) are already excluded. The rate improved from 64.6% on the earlier, smaller dataset.

## Where the misses come from

Of those 406 misses, **365** fall inside the window the raw Nedap export covers (it ends 2026-08-27); the other 41 were diagnosed after it. Within the checkable slice:

- **221 were never flagged by the camera at all** — genuine detection misses
- **144 were flagged, but the flag never reached DairyComp**

That second group looked like a pipeline problem. Checking it against the enrollment rules shows part of it isn't:

- 13 had every flag land inside its own `FTDAT` window
- 28 were `LOW`-only flags on cows with upper-leg lameness history, which blocks the `Low` route
- **36 of the 144 were the system working as designed, leaving 108 as real pipeline losses**

A separate check found **31 of the 406 misses involve a cow missing from the SmartSight platform entirely** — she was never being watched. Staff did not backstop these either: only **76 of 406 (18.7%)** had a staff lameness check in the week before diagnosis.

One judgement call sits behind the pipeline figure: 1,422 flags are marked "not completed" in the raw export and are counted here as the camera having flagged the cow. 27 of the 144 pipeline losses rest only on such a flag — counting completed flags alone would give 117.

## What the camera is missing: DD on a hind foot

This is the most actionable result in the report, and the fuller data sharpened it.

Comparing the 221 detection misses against the 384 cases the camera did flag, neither lesion type nor foot alone explains the gap — but crossing them does:

| Lesion and foot | % of misses | % of flagged | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DD on a rear foot** | 39.4 | 24.5 | **+14.9** |
| DD on a front foot | 8.1 | 7.6 | +0.5 |
| Anything else on a rear foot | 32.1 | 41.7 | **−9.6** |

- **Front-foot DD shows no gap at all**, so this is not about digital dermatitis as such.
- **Non-DD lesions on a hind foot are caught *better* than average**, so it is not about hind feet either.
- The blind spot is the **combination**: digital dermatitis on a hind foot.

This held as the dataset nearly doubled, and the gap widened slightly.

One likely reason, though this data can't prove it: DD is often bilateral, and a cow sore on both hind feet walks symmetrically. A camera scoring mobility off asymmetry would be expected to under-detect exactly that. Worth putting to Nedap directly.

## Data currency — read Q1 with care

The three feeds are pulled separately and don't end on the same date:

| Feed | Covers to |
|---|---|
| DairyComp events | 2026-09-07 |
| Nedap sensor flags | 2026-08-27 |
| **Milk** | **2026-08-04** |

Milk is the problem. A cow needs 30 days of records after her alert to appear at the right-hand end of the milk curves, so **334 of the 939 cohort cows contribute no milk at all, and the day-30 figures rest on 282 cows.** Those figures describe the earlier-alerting cows, not the pilot as a whole, and will move as milk data catches up. Milk will always lag the rest of the report by about a month by construction.

## For discussion

- **The biggest single category is genuine detection misses (221 of 365 checkable), not data problems.** That is a sensitivity question for Nedap and shouldn't get lost behind the pipeline story.
- **The miss has a specific shape: DD on a hind foot.** A concrete, testable question for Nedap — does an asymmetry-based mobility score under-detect bilateral hind-foot disease? Front-foot DD and non-DD hind-foot lesions both come out fine, which makes this hard to explain any other way.
- **Pipeline losses are real: 108 after accounting for by-design suppression.** Worth taking to the integration team.
- **The batch-load timing issue affects 170 of 1,109 alerts (15.3%).** Entering trim data the same day would remove most of it.
- **Auto-trimming gets cows seen faster but trims a lot of sound feet** — 54.1% of TX's first visits find no lesion. That is the cost side of the protocol.
- **Culling and staff-detection rates are now indistinguishable between arms.** With 14 weeks and ~50 culls, the honest read is that neither shows an effect rather than that a small one is hiding.
- **Next data pull: milk.** It is the only feed materially behind, and it is the one gating a real read on production.
